newsitem.title: USA: Mideast summit failure raises questions.
newsitem.headline: Mideast summit failure raises questions.

text.p: The Middle East summit failed to achieve substantive gains, raising the question of whether President Bill Clinton squandered the power of his office in bringing Israeli and Palestinian leaders to Washington.

Following the two-day meeting there were fears that violence between Israelis and Palestinians could re-ignite. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu made no concessions -- he insisted beforehand he would not -- and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat essentially went home empty-handed.

There was no hint that Clinton -- warned by his Republican challenger Bob Dole not to pressure Israel -- had in any serious way tried to use his presidential muscle to move Netanyahu toward a significant deal.
To be sure the meeting was not without some merit.

According to Clinton, who tried desperately to put the best face on his high-risk gamble, Netanyahu and Arafat committed themselves to a non-violent future and to resume immediate peace talks on Sunday at the Erez border crossing between the Jewish state and Palestinian-run Gaza.

But there was no deal on when the talks would end or when Israel would implement long-delayed aspects of its 1993 peace accord with the Palestinians, including redeployment of Israeli troops in the West Bank town of Hebron due last March.

These remained critical issues for Palestinians who, frustrated by Netanyahu's failure to live up to the 1993 accord, erupted in rage and violence last week when Israel opened a tunnel in Jerusalem near Moslem and Jewish holy sites.
The two sides agreed the resumed peace talks should focus first on Hebron and run continuously -- essentially affirming a proposal Netanyahu espoused on his way to Washington.
The mere idea of talks basically favoured Israel because Arafat simply wanted Israel to withdraw the Hebron troops and comply with the 1993 agreement.

The gap between the two sides was in full view during a closing White House press conference in which Clinton did all the talking and the other principals -- Netanyahu and Arafat -- sat stiffly to the side. Both Mideast leaders were poker-faced but Arafat seemed especially glum.
Afterward Israel hailed the summit as a victory while a senior Palestinian negotiator called the meeting a failure.
Richard Haass, a Mideast adviser to ex-President George Bush, said of the summit, "The Americans have little to show for it except for a commitment to keep talking."
Haass, now with Brookings Institution, told Reuters the administration "paid a large price in terms of an awful lot of American involvement."

"The danger now is you may have squandered American diplomatic capital and you raised expectations and don't have a lot to show for it ... Any time you get the president of the United States involved, you inherently raise expectations."
While Clinton hosted the summit and previously claimed some credit for the Israel-Palestinian accords, his involvement in the current crisis seemed minimal.

Last week he left it to Secretary of State Warren Christopher to try to bring the two leaders into telephone communication or get them to hold a summit in the Middle East. When that failed Clinton invited them to Washington.

Clinton met for somewhat longer than two hours with Netanyahu and Arafat on Tuesday and again on Wednesday for about an hour. That was a far cry from the 13 days President Jimmy Carter spent achieving the Israel-Egypt Camp David Accords in 1978.
Clinton was in no position to devote that kind of time to the effort even if he wanted to. He was to hold his first debate with Dole on Sunday and needed time to prepare.
U.S. officials insisted they had no choice but to call the summit if they wanted to save the peace process launched in 1991, even if it was unlikely a breakthrough could result.

Jim Zogby, head of the Arab-American Institute and an adviser to Clinton's campaign, expressed disappointment at the summit results but blamed Netanyahu who he believed still had not made the decision to fulfil the 1993 peace accords.

He said Clinton had to call the summit to try to defuse Israeli-Palestinian tensions and absolved him for not taking a tougher stand toward Netanyahu because of political realities -- Dole's attacks and an election five weeks away.
Zogby and other experts stressed the need for quick action on the negotiations resuming at Erez on Sunday so that the Palestinian tinderbox did not explode again.

Said Jonathan Jacoby of the Israel Policy Forum: "I think the jury is still out on the summit. The summit is not over. The first part is over ... (But) if they (leaders) take too long and are unable to give Palestinians and Israel some assurance there is an agreement at hand, then frustration will rise again."
